# The whole-tree comparison is the wrong scope, found by the slice that implemented it

RED is record 6 and GREEN is record 7, 16 failed then 49 passed, and the work is sound: `cited_check`
compares a recorded fingerprint instead of an attempt number, the ordering line is untouched, and the
refusals are three distinct sentences rather than one doing four jobs. The full suite is 1,129 tests.

**But the rule as I specified it in record 4 cannot do the job the ticket exists for, and the implementer
said so rather than widening it to fit.** The solution record said to compare the cited check's recorded
`after` fingerprint against the tree the citing record is written against. That is a whole-tree comparison,
and the measurement it reported kills it: every green records a distinct tree. SEEN-107 has 13 greens across
13 distinct trees, SEEN-109 13 across 13, SEEN-111 5 across 5. So an earlier attempt's green can equal the
tree at the final advance only if nothing at all changed since, which is never true on a ticket whose later
slices added code. On SEEN-112's real journal the citations stay refused, now by the fingerprint sentence
instead of the attempt one, which is a better message for the same wrong answer.

The scope is the defect, not the mechanism. "Is this evidence still about this code" means the code **that
check covered**, which is the files its slice names, and not every file in the repository. A green proving
slice 1 is still evidence about slice 1 when slice 3 has since added code somewhere else; it stops being
evidence the moment slice 1's own files move. The ticket's own description says as much, "whether the
evidence is still about this code", and I wrote the narrower reading into the solution record by accident.

So the plan is amended rather than the rule bent: the comparison is scoped to the files the cited check's
slice names, read from the route or the accepted plan that named them, and the whole-tree comparison
survives only as the fallback when a citation cannot be attributed to a slice at all. The mirror case must
still refuse: a green whose own slice's files have changed is not evidence any more, and
`EvidenceForChangedCode` becomes a test about a covered file rather than about any file.

**The second divergence, which I accept as the better rule rather than treat as a deviation.**
`ReplanCarriesForward` was satisfied by plan identity rather than by a fingerprint: `plan_accepted_at` now
returns the first acceptance of the plan that still stands, walking back over acceptances whose slices agree
with the current plan on every slice the two have in common. The implementer diverged from "judged the same
way as above" for a reason it could check and I had not: neither caller can supply a tree, because
`cli.build_pack` passes no repository to `handoff.pack` and `guard.decide` passes only records, and both
files are outside the slice. And a whole-tree comparison there would have carried forward only the single
most recent green, so SEEN-112's state at its record 44 would read "1 of 3" and still hand out the wrong
slice. Plan identity is journal-only, exact, and narrower than counting everything, and
`test_a_replan_that_changed_the_slices_starts_its_own_count` pins the case that must still restart. It is
adopted into the amended record instead of being left for a reviewer to query.

**What the sweep proved and what it did not.** All 26 journals under `docs/harness/history/`, 265 citations
examined, no verdict moves. The reason matters: none of the 265 was cross-attempt or cross-stage, because
the old rule made such a citation impossible to record. So the sweep proves no delivered evidence is
revived. It does not prove the old rule never bit: what it cost is invisible, in tickets that re-proved work
or lost a criterion rather than in refusals anybody can read.
